patients.label: 59-year-old man with acute rotational vertigo mimicking vestibular neuritis, later attributed to labyrinthine infarction

identity_evidence.quote: We report the case of a 59-year-old man who presented

attribution_limitations: Hearing statements differ in wording and are not reconciled: no current hearing loss reported at presentation, a 2013 history of left sudden sensorineural hearing loss not explored nor rehabilitated, severe left sensorineural hearing loss on later tonal audiometry, subtotal left deafness in the Figure 4 caption for the same audiometry, and a discussion sentence saying the patient already had profound deafness in that ear without naming the ear. None is treated as a source conflict: the presentation statement is a reported symptom, the 2013 loss and the audiometry are different time points, severe and subtotal are two severity words for one audiogram rather than two values, and the discussion sentence is kept review_only. No pre-existing deafness or its side is inferred.

The treatment is described as high doses of corticosteroids with methylprednisolone 120 mg per day, while the discussion says the embolism happened after only one dose of 120 mg of methylprednisolone. Both are kept; the number of doses given is not inferred. The sentence also states an intravenous route once for the corticosteroids, antiemetic therapy and acetylleucine, so route is attributed only to methylprednisolone.

Left vestibular neuritis was the retained first diagnosis, and the case is called a labyrinthine infarction mimicking peripheral vestibular neuritis. The source does not say misdiagnosed, so the neuritis is kept provisional rather than refuted. The authors also discuss whether the corticosteroid provoked the stroke and say evidence is lacking; no causal link between the treatment and the infarction is recorded.

The text says there was no opacification at the angiographic sequences without naming the vessel, while the Figure 1 caption says the left vertebral artery is obliterated on the MRI angiography sequence. The two statements are kept as separate facts and not merged.

The paragraph reporting the reassessment 10 days later states the time in its first sentence only. The Romberg and nystagmus sentence is linked to that reassessment event but carries no time of its own, and the Video Head Impulse Test, posturography and audiometry sentences do not repeat the time, so those investigations are a separate untimed event whose order relative to the reassessment and to the transfer is not stated.

The discussion states that the patient had no other vascular factor than arterial hypertension under treatment, while the limitations say important laboratory work to rule out other vascular risk factors was lacking. No absence of other risk factors is recorded as a fact.

The 24 h later for the headaches follows the sentence on improvement but names no anchor event; the timing is recorded as after with no anchor, and Figure 2 prints anterior semicircular canal gains that appear only in the image, so the text records them as normal.

The case text says the embolic vertebral artery caused the labyrinthine infarction responsible for the acute left vestibular deficit present at presentation, while the discussion says the vascular embolism happened after only one dose of methylprednisolone. No order between the corticosteroid treatment and the infarction is recorded.

The Figure 3 caption says the visual and vestibular inputs were absent, while the text names only the absent vestibular input with visual dependency at 100%. The caption-only absent visual input is kept as its own fact.
